name: Realtime Voice Agents and Latency Budgets
question: How fast must a voice agent answer, and in which language?
summary: A voice agent either chains speech-to-text, an LLM and text-to-speech, or uses a speech-to-speech model. Callers expect a reply within about 600 ms of finishing; beyond 1.5 s the call feels broken. Every stage streams, turn detection decides when the caller has finished, and callers must be able to interrupt. In India the harder problem is language: accuracy in Hindi is far better than in Bhojpuri or Maithili, code-mixed Hinglish is the norm, and phone audio degrades recognition further.
useCases: Customer-service helplines in Hindi and regional languages
steps: Measure latency from the end of the caller’s speech to first audio
Use smart turn detection and streaming at every stage
Choose speech models evaluated on your callers’ languages and phone audio
Allow barge-in and hand over to a person when confidence is low
pitfalls: Silence-based turn detection that waits 800 ms
Choosing speech-to-text on clean benchmarks rather than real calls
No human fallback for low-resource languages
tools: OpenAI Realtime API and Gemini Live API
remember: Stream everything, detect turns smartly, test on real callers.

steps.title: Measure the right gap
steps.text: Latency is timed from the end of the caller’s speech to the first audio back. The pilot took about 1.9 seconds, and 1 in 6 callers hung up.

steps.title: Stream every stage
steps.text: Speech-to-text runs while the caller talks, the model streams tokens, and synthesis starts on the first words. A fast model keeps the first token quick.

steps.title: Choose speech models on real calls
steps.text: A general model got 1 word in 5 wrong on Hinglish phone calls; an India-tuned model tested on recorded calls did far better.

steps.title: Detect turns smartly
steps.text: Waiting for 800 ms of silence adds most of a second. A turn-detection model decides sooner and lets callers interrupt.

steps.title: Short, natural replies
steps.text: One or two short sentences in the caller’s own mix of Hindi and English sound natural and finish sooner.

steps.title: Know when to hand over
steps.text: Recognition is much weaker in Bhojpuri and Maithili. When confidence is low, the agent asks once, then transfers to a person.

practice.scenario: A fictional bank piloted a Hindi and Hinglish voice agent for card blocking and UPI dispute status. The first build waited for 800 ms of silence, used a general speech model and did not stream speech synthesis: replies took almost 2 seconds and 1 in 6 callers hung up. Smart turn detection, an India-tuned speech model tested on real phone calls and streaming at every stage brought replies to about 700 ms. Callers speaking Bhojpuri or Maithili are offered a person.

industries.use: Card blocking, balance and dispute-status helplines

practice.analogy: A good phone operator: answers quickly, lets you interrupt, understands how you actually speak, and hands you to a colleague who speaks your language when needed.

library.name: LiveKit Agents
library.what: A realtime voice framework: pluggable speech-to-text, LLM and speech synthesis, voice activity detection, a multilingual turn detector and telephony.

practice.note: Plugin and model names are examples; check current docs. Measure latency from the end of the caller’s speech to first audio on real calls.

samples.code:
from livekit import agents
from livekit.agents import Agent, AgentSession
from livekit.plugins import openai, sarvam, silero
from livekit.plugins.turn_detector.multilingual import MultilingualModel

class Helpline(Agent):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(instructions=(
            "You are a bank helpline agent. Reply in the caller's language and "
            "register (Hindi, Hinglish or English) in one or two short sentences. "
            "Never read out full card or account numbers. If you are not sure "
            "what the caller said, ask once, then transfer to a person."))

async def entrypoint(ctx: agents.JobContext):
    session = AgentSession(
        stt=sarvam.STT(language="hi-IN"),        # tested on real phone audio
        llm=openai.LLM(model="gpt-4.1-mini"),    # a fast model; example name
        tts=sarvam.TTS(target_language_code="hi-IN"),
        vad=silero.VAD.load(),
        turn_detection=MultilingualModel())      # smarter than silence alone
    await session.start(room=ctx.room, agent=Helpline())
    await session.generate_reply(instructions="Greet the caller in Hindi.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    agents.cli.run_app(agents.WorkerOptions(entrypoint_fnc=entrypoint))

numericDrill.question: A cascaded voice agent has network 60 ms, end-of-turn detection 250 ms, speech-to-text finalisation 120 ms, LLM first token 200 ms and speech synthesis first audio 150 ms. What is the total from the end of the caller’s speech to first audio, in ms?
numericDrill.answer: 60 + 250 + 120 + 200 + 150 = 780 ms, inside the acceptable 500–800 ms range. Waiting for 800 ms of silence instead of smart turn detection would add 550 ms and push it past 1.3 seconds.

interview.question: How do you get a voice agent under 800 ms?
interview.answer: Stream every stage so speech-to-text runs while the caller talks and synthesis starts on the first words of the reply; use smart turn detection rather than long silence timeouts; pick a fast model for the first response; keep servers close to the telephony provider; and consider speech-to-speech models where their language coverage is good enough.

interview.question: What is different about voice agents for Indian customers?
interview.answer: Callers mix Hindi and English, switch languages mid-sentence and call over narrowband phone lines. Recognition is far better for Hindi than for Bhojpuri, Maithili and other lower-resource languages. Evaluate speech models on real calls in each language, handle code-mixed text, and route callers to a person when recognition confidence is low.
